cards.title: In a fraction $\frac{a}{b}$, what do the **denominator** $b$ and the **numerator** $a$ each tell you?
cards.body:
The denominator $b$ is how many equal parts the whole is cut into; the numerator $a$ is how many of those parts you have.

A **fraction** is a number written as one whole number over another, like $\frac{3}{4}$. The bottom number names the size of the pieces (fourths, fifths, eighths); the top number counts them.

Example: a pizza cut into 4 equal slices, with 3 slices eaten, is $\frac{3}{4}$ of the pizza gone.

Watch out: the pieces must be equal. Three slices out of four unequal slices is not $\frac{3}{4}$. Also, $b$ can never be 0, because you cannot cut something into zero parts.

Mnemonic: **D**enominator is **D**own at the bottom, and it names the pieces.
cards.searchQuery: numerator denominator meaning fraction parts of a whole

cards.title: Besides "parts of a whole", what are two other ways to read $\frac{a}{b}$ (with $b \neq 0$)?
cards.body:
As the division $a \div b$, and as a point on the number line: cut each unit step into $b$ equal pieces and move $a$ pieces to the right of 0.

Why: share 3 pizzas equally among 4 people. Cut every pizza into 4 slices; each person takes one slice from each pizza, which is 3 slices, or $\frac{3}{4}$ of a pizza. So $3 \div 4 = \frac{3}{4}$.

Example: $\frac{3}{4}$ sits three quarter-steps to the right of 0, between 0 and 1. The fraction $-\frac{3}{4}$ sits the same distance to the left of 0.

Key idea: a fraction bar is a division sign in disguise, and every fraction is a point on the number line.
cards.searchQuery: fraction as division and as a point on the number line

cards.title: How do you write $\frac{a}{b}$ in **simplest form** using $g$, the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$?
cards.body:
Divide the top and the bottom by $g$: $\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{a \div g}{b \div g}$.

Two fractions are **equivalent fractions** when they name the same number, like $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{3}{6}$. Multiplying or dividing the top and bottom by the same nonzero number always gives an equivalent fraction. A fraction is in **simplest form** when its numerator and denominator are relatively prime, that is, when their greatest common divisor is 1.

Example: the greatest common divisor of 18 and 30 is 6, so $\frac{18}{30} = \frac{18 \div 6}{30 \div 6} = \frac{3}{5}$.

Watch out: dividing by a common divisor that is not the greatest only gets you part of the way. Dividing $\frac{18}{30}$ by 2 gives $\frac{9}{15}$, which can still be reduced.
cards.searchQuery: reduce fraction simplest form greatest common divisor

cards.title: Convert the improper fraction $\frac{17}{5}$ to a mixed number.
cards.body:
$3\frac{2}{5}$

A **mixed number** is a whole number and a fraction written side by side: $3\frac{2}{5}$ means $3 + \frac{2}{5}$. An **improper fraction** has a numerator at least as big as its denominator, so its value is 1 or more.

Example: divide 17 by 5. You get 3 with remainder 2, so there are 3 whole ones and 2 fifths left over: $3\frac{2}{5}$.

To go back, multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator: $3 \cdot 5 + 2 = 17$, so $3\frac{2}{5} = \frac{17}{5}$.

Watch out: $3\frac{2}{5}$ means 3 plus $\frac{2}{5}$, not 3 times $\frac{2}{5}$.
cards.searchQuery: convert improper fraction to mixed number 17/5

cards.title: Which is larger, $\frac{5}{8}$ or $\frac{7}{12}$? Give the larger fraction.
cards.body:
$\frac{5}{8}$

Rewrite both over a common denominator. The least common multiple of 8 and 12 is 24, so $\frac{5}{8} = \frac{15}{24}$ and $\frac{7}{12} = \frac{14}{24}$. Since $15 > 14$, $\frac{5}{8}$ is larger.

Tip: cross-multiplication is a shortcut. Compare $5 \cdot 12 = 60$ with $8 \cdot 7 = 56$. The side with the bigger product has the bigger fraction, so $\frac{5}{8}$ wins.

Why it works: cross-multiplying is the same as rewriting both fractions over the denominator $8 \cdot 12 = 96$, where they become $\frac{60}{96}$ and $\frac{56}{96}$. (This shortcut is for positive fractions.)
cards.searchQuery: compare fractions common denominator cross multiplication

cards.title: Why is the belief "$\frac{1}{8}$ is bigger than $\frac{1}{5}$ because 8 is bigger than 5" false?
cards.body:
A bigger denominator cuts the whole into more pieces, so each piece is smaller: $\frac{1}{8} < \frac{1}{5}$.

Why: picture two identical pizzas, one cut into 8 slices and one into 5. A slice of the 5-slice pizza is clearly the bigger slice.

Watch out: this rule only holds when the numerators match. With different numerators you can't judge by the denominators alone: $\frac{3}{8} = \frac{15}{40}$ is bigger than $\frac{1}{5} = \frac{8}{40}$.

Tip: when in doubt, rewrite both fractions over a common denominator and compare the numerators.
cards.searchQuery: larger denominator smaller fraction misconception unit fractions

cards.title: What is the **least common denominator** (LCD) of two fractions?
cards.body:
The least common multiple of their denominators.

A **common denominator** is any number that both denominators divide into evenly, which means any common multiple of them. The **least common denominator** is the smallest one.

Example: for $\frac{5}{6}$ and $\frac{3}{4}$, the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, and 4 divides 12 evenly, so the LCD is 12.

Watch out: multiplying the denominators ($6 \cdot 4 = 24$) always gives a common denominator, but it can be bigger than needed and leads to more reducing later.

Tip: find the LCM from prime factorizations when the denominators are large.
cards.searchQuery: least common denominator lcd least common multiple fractions

cards.title: Add or subtract fractions with the same denominator: $\dfrac{a}{n} \pm \dfrac{c}{n} = \,?$
cards.body:
$\dfrac{a \pm c}{n}$

Add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator.

Why: the pieces are all the same size, so you just count pieces. 2 fifths plus 1 fifth is 3 fifths, which is $\frac{2}{5} + \frac{1}{5} = \frac{3}{5}$.

Example: $\frac{7}{10} - \frac{3}{10} = \frac{4}{10} = \frac{2}{5}$.

Watch out: the denominator does not change, because the size of the pieces does not change. If the denominators differ, first rewrite the fractions over a common denominator.
cards.searchQuery: add subtract fractions same denominator rule

cards.title: Compute $\frac{5}{6} + \frac{3}{4}$ using the least common denominator, and write the result as a mixed number.
cards.body:
$1\frac{7}{12}$

The LCD of 6 and 4 is 12.

1. Rewrite each fraction over 12: $\frac{5}{6} = \frac{10}{12}$ and $\frac{3}{4} = \frac{9}{12}$.
2. Add the numerators: $\frac{10}{12} + \frac{9}{12} = \frac{19}{12}$.
3. Convert to a mixed number: $\frac{19}{12} = 1\frac{7}{12}$.

Tip: always check whether the result can be reduced. Here 19 is prime, so $\frac{19}{12}$ is already in simplest form.
cards.searchQuery: add fractions different denominators 5/6 + 3/4 example

cards.title: Multiply two fractions: $\dfrac{a}{b} \cdot \dfrac{c}{d} = \,?$ (with $b, d \neq 0$)
cards.body:
$\dfrac{a \cdot c}{b \cdot d}$

Multiply the tops together and the bottoms together. No common denominator is needed.

Why: $\frac{1}{2}$ of $\frac{1}{3}$ of a pizza means cutting each third in half, which gives 6 equal pieces in the whole pizza and takes one of them: $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{6}$.

Tip: cancel common divisors between any top and any bottom before multiplying. For $\frac{8}{9} \cdot \frac{3}{10}$, cancel 2 from 8 and 10 and 3 from 9 and 3: you get $\frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{5} = \frac{4}{15}$.
cards.searchQuery: multiply fractions rule cancel before multiplying

cards.title: Why does dividing by $\frac{c}{d}$ (with $c \neq 0$) give the same result as multiplying by its **reciprocal** $\frac{d}{c}$?
cards.body:
Dividing by a number undoes multiplying by it, and the reciprocal $\frac{d}{c}$ is the number that multiplies with $\frac{c}{d}$ to give 1.

The **reciprocal** of a fraction is the fraction turned upside down. A fraction and its reciprocal multiply to 1: $\frac{c}{d} \cdot \frac{d}{c} = 1$.

Why: dividing by $\frac{1}{2}$ asks "how many halves fit?" There are 2 halves in each whole, so $3 \div \frac{1}{2} = 3 \cdot 2 = 6$. In general, $\frac{a}{b} \div \frac{c}{d} = \frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{d}{c}$.

Watch out: flip only the fraction you divide by, never the first one. Zero has no reciprocal.
cards.searchQuery: why dividing by a fraction means multiplying by reciprocal

cards.title: Compute $2\frac{1}{3} \div \left(-\frac{7}{9}\right)$. Type a whole number or a fraction such as 1/2.
cards.body:
$-3$

1. Turn the mixed number into an improper fraction: $2\frac{1}{3} = \frac{7}{3}$.
2. Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor: $\frac{7}{3} \cdot \left(-\frac{9}{7}\right)$.
3. Cancel the 7s: $\frac{1}{3} \cdot (-9)$, and $9 \div 3 = 3$.
4. A positive divided by a negative is negative, so the answer is $-3$.

Check: $-3 \cdot \left(-\frac{7}{9}\right) = \frac{21}{9} = \frac{7}{3} = 2\frac{1}{3}$.

Watch out: never multiply with a mixed number as it stands. Convert it first.
cards.searchQuery: divide mixed number by negative fraction worked example

cards.title: Simplify the **complex fraction** $\dfrac{1 + \frac{1}{2}}{2 - \frac{1}{4}}$ to a single fraction in simplest form.
cards.body:
$\frac{6}{7}$

A **complex fraction** has fractions in its numerator, its denominator, or both. The fraction bar means divide: top $\div$ bottom.

1. Simplify the top: $1 + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}$.
2. Simplify the bottom: $2 - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{8}{4} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{7}{4}$.
3. Divide: $\frac{3}{2} \div \frac{7}{4} = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{4}{7} = \frac{12}{14} = \frac{6}{7}$.

Watch out: finish the addition and subtraction on top and bottom first. Do not cancel pieces of a sum, like the $\frac{1}{2}$ against the $\frac{1}{4}$.
cards.searchQuery: simplify complex fraction numerator denominator fractions

cards.title: Why is "add the tops and add the bottoms", as in $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{5}$, wrong?
cards.body:
Fractions add only when the pieces are the same size; the correct sum is $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{6}$.

Why: halves and thirds are different sizes, so you can't count them together. Over the common denominator 6 you get $\frac{3}{6} + \frac{2}{6} = \frac{5}{6}$.

Watch out: a quick sanity check catches the error. $\frac{2}{5}$ is smaller than $\frac{1}{2}$, but adding a positive amount to $\frac{1}{2}$ can't make it smaller.
cards.searchQuery: common mistake adding fractions numerators and denominators

cards.title: What is a **decimal**, and what do the first three places after the **decimal point** stand for?
cards.body:
A decimal writes a number in base ten with a decimal point separating the whole part from the fractional part; the first three places after the point are tenths, hundredths and thousandths.

Each place is worth one tenth of the place to its left, just as in whole numbers.

Example: $0.375$ is 3 tenths, 7 hundredths and 5 thousandths: $\frac{3}{10} + \frac{7}{100} + \frac{5}{1000} = \frac{375}{1000}$. Dividing top and bottom by their greatest common divisor, 125, gives $\frac{3}{8}$.

Tip: to turn a decimal into a fraction, put its digits over 1 followed by as many zeros as there are places after the point, then reduce.
cards.searchQuery: decimal place value tenths hundredths thousandths decimal point

cards.title: Why is it wrong to add decimals by lining up their right-hand ends, as in $0.5 + 0.25 = 0.30$?
cards.body:
You must add digits of the same place value, so line up the decimal points: $0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75$.

Why: 5 tenths and 5 hundredths are different-sized pieces, just like halves and thirds. Right-aligning adds the 5 tenths to the 5 hundredths and gives the nonsense 0.30.

Example: write $0.50$ above $0.25$. Tenths line up with tenths and hundredths with hundredths: $50 + 25 = 75$ hundredths, so $0.75$.

Tip: add zeros on the right to give every number the same number of places. Subtraction works the same way.
cards.searchQuery: adding decimals line up decimal points mistake

cards.title: To multiply two decimals, how do you place the decimal point in the product?
cards.body:
Multiply them as whole numbers, then give the product as many decimal places as the two numbers you multiplied have together.

Example: $0.35 \cdot 0.4$. Multiply $35 \cdot 4 = 140$. The numbers have $2 + 1 = 3$ decimal places in all, so the product is $0.140 = 0.14$.

Why: $0.35 = \frac{35}{100}$ and $0.4 = \frac{4}{10}$, so the product is $\frac{140}{1000}$, which is 140 thousandths.

Watch out: this is not the rule for adding. For multiplication you count places; you do not line up the points.
cards.searchQuery: multiply decimals count decimal places rule

cards.title: Compute $7.2 \div 0.045$. Type the number.
cards.body:
$160$

Move the decimal point in both numbers by the same amount until the divisor is a whole number. Here three places does it: $7.2 \div 0.045 = 7200 \div 45 = 160$.

Why: $\frac{7.2}{0.045} = \frac{7200}{45}$, because multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by 1000 gives an equivalent fraction.

Check: $45 \cdot 160 = 7200$. Correct.

Watch out: move the point the same number of places in both numbers. Moving just one changes the answer.
cards.searchQuery: divide decimals by decimal move decimal point worked example

cards.title: Write $\frac{7}{12}$ as a decimal by dividing 7 by 12.
cards.body:
$0.58333\ldots = 0.58\overline{3}$

A fraction is a division, so use long division: $70 \div 12 = 5$ remainder 10, then $100 \div 12 = 8$ remainder 4, then $40 \div 12 = 3$ remainder 4. The remainder 4 keeps coming back, so the digit 3 repeats forever.

A decimal whose digits stop is a **terminating decimal**: $\frac{3}{8} = 0.375$. A decimal whose digits repeat forever in a pattern is a **repeating decimal**, and a bar marks the repeating block: $0.58\overline{3}$.

Key idea: dividing the top by the bottom always ends either in a remainder of 0, which gives a terminating decimal, or in a repeating remainder, which gives a repeating decimal.
cards.searchQuery: fraction to decimal long division repeating decimal 7/12

cards.title: When does a fraction in simplest form have a terminating decimal?
cards.body:
Exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5.

Why: a terminating decimal is a fraction over 10, 100, 1000 and so on, and those numbers have only 2 and 5 as prime factors. If the denominator is made of 2s and 5s, multiply the top and bottom to turn it into such a number. Conversely, if a fraction in simplest form equals a whole number over 10, 100, 1000 and so on, its denominator divides that power of ten, so it has no prime factors other than 2 and 5.

Example: $\frac{3}{40}$ terminates, since $40 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 5$: $\frac{3}{40} = \frac{75}{1000} = 0.075$. But $\frac{1}{6}$ does not, since $6 = 2 \cdot 3$: it is $0.1666\ldots$.

Watch out: reduce first. $\frac{6}{15}$ has a 3 in its denominator, but it equals $\frac{2}{5} = 0.4$, which terminates.
cards.searchQuery: terminating decimal denominator only prime factors 2 and 5

cards.title: Write the repeating decimal $0.\overline{B}$ as a fraction, where the repeating block $B$ is written with $k$ digits (leading zeros count, as in $0.\overline{05}$).
cards.body:
$\dfrac{B}{99\ldots9}$, with $k$ nines in the denominator; then reduce.

Example: $0.\overline{36} = \frac{36}{99} = \frac{4}{11}$, and $0.\overline{3} = \frac{3}{9} = \frac{1}{3}$.

Why: call the number $N = 0.363636\ldots$. Then $100N = 36.363636\ldots$. Subtracting, the endless tails cancel: $99N = 36$, so $N = \frac{36}{99}$.

Watch out: this works when the repeating starts right after the decimal point. For $0.58\overline{3}$ the 58 comes first, so you need an extra step to handle it.
cards.searchQuery: repeating decimal to fraction block over nines

cards.title: What is a **ratio**, and how do you simplify one?
cards.body:
A ratio compares quantities of the same kind by division: $a : b$ means $\frac{a}{b}$, and order matters. Simplify by dividing every part by their greatest common divisor.

Example: 6 red marbles to 9 blue marbles is $6 : 9 = 2 : 3$.

A ratio can compare three quantities too. $12 : 18 : 30$ has greatest common divisor 6, so it simplifies to $2 : 3 : 5$.

Watch out: order matters. Red to blue is $2 : 3$, but blue to red is $3 : 2$.
cards.searchQuery: what is a ratio simplify ratio three-way ratio
refs: AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 7 (Ratios, Conversions, and Rates)

cards.title: What is a **rate**, and what is a **unit rate**?
cards.body:
A rate compares two quantities with different units; a unit rate is a rate whose second quantity is exactly 1 unit.

Example: 150 miles in 3 hours is a rate. Divide to get the unit rate: $\frac{150}{3} = 50$ miles per hour.

Use unit rates to compare. A 12-ounce jar for $3.60$ dollars costs $0.30$ dollars per ounce. A 20-ounce jar for $5.50$ dollars costs $0.275$ dollars per ounce, so the larger jar is the better buy.

Tip: to compare prices or speeds, always reduce each to a rate "per 1".
cards.searchQuery: rate unit rate definition unit price comparison
refs: AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 7 (Ratios, Conversions, and Rates)

cards.title: What is a **proportion**, and what does it say about two ratios?
cards.body:
A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal: $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$.

Why it works: if 3 cups of flour make 20 cookies, then 6 cups make 40. Doubling both amounts keeps the ratio the same: $\frac{3}{20} = \frac{6}{40}$. Proportions describe two quantities that grow together in lockstep, like recipe amounts, steady speed, or price per item.

Watch out: this only fits steady relationships. A taxi fare with a flat starting fee plus a charge per mile is not proportional, because doubling the miles does not double the fare.
cards.searchQuery: proportion definition equal ratios recipe scaling
refs: AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 7 (Ratios, Conversions, and Rates)

cards.title: **Cross-multiplication**: if $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$ (with $b, d \neq 0$), what product statement follows?
cards.body:
$a \cdot d = b \cdot c$

Why: rewrite both fractions over the common denominator $b \cdot d$. They become $\frac{a \cdot d}{b \cdot d}$ and $\frac{b \cdot c}{b \cdot d}$. Equal fractions with the same denominator have equal numerators.

Example: if $\frac{3}{20} = \frac{n}{50}$ for an unknown number $n$, then $3 \cdot 50 = 20 \cdot n$, so $150 = 20n$ and $n = 7.5$ (since $20 \cdot 7.5 = 150$).

Watch out: cross-multiplying works only when one fraction is set equal to one fraction. It does not apply to sums like $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}$.
cards.searchQuery: cross multiplication proportion rule ad = bc
refs: AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 7 (Ratios, Conversions, and Rates)

cards.title: Using a **conversion factor** and $1\ \text{in} = 2.54\ \text{cm}$, convert 10 inches to centimeters.
cards.body:
$25.4\ \text{cm}$

A conversion factor is a fraction equal to 1, built from two measures that are equal, such as $\frac{2.54\ \text{cm}}{1\ \text{in}} = 1$. Multiplying by 1 changes the unit but not the amount.

$$10\ \text{in} \cdot \frac{2.54\ \text{cm}}{1\ \text{in}} = 25.4\ \text{cm}$$

Tip: put the unit you want to get rid of on the bottom, so it cancels. Inches cancel, and centimeters remain.
cards.searchQuery: conversion factor unit conversion inches to centimeters
refs: AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 7 (Ratios, Conversions, and Rates)

cards.title: A car travels at 90 kilometers per hour. How many meters per second is that? Type the number.
cards.body:
$25$

Chain conversion factors, each equal to 1, so that kilometers and hours cancel:

$$\frac{90\ \text{km}}{1\ \text{h}} \cdot \frac{1000\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{km}} \cdot \frac{1\ \text{h}}{3600\ \text{s}} = \frac{90000}{3600}\ \text{m/s} = 25\ \text{m/s}$$

Check: 25 meters per second for 3600 seconds covers $25 \cdot 3600 = 90000$ meters, which is 90 kilometers in one hour.

Tip: to go from km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6, because $3600 \div 1000 = 3.6$.
cards.searchQuery: convert km/h to m/s conversion factors 90 km/h
refs: AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 7 (Ratios, Conversions, and Rates)

cards.title: A class has boys and girls in the ratio $3 : 5$. Why is it wrong to say boys are $\frac{3}{5}$ of the class?
cards.body:
The ratio $3 : 5$ compares boys to girls (part to part); boys are $\frac{3}{3+5} = \frac{3}{8}$ of the class.

Example: in every group of 8 students there are 3 boys and 5 girls. With 24 students that is 9 boys and 15 girls. Boys are $\frac{9}{24} = \frac{3}{8}$ of the class, while $\frac{9}{15} = \frac{3}{5}$ compares boys with girls.

Tip: to get a part-to-whole fraction, add the parts of the ratio to find the whole.
cards.searchQuery: part to part ratio versus part to whole fraction
refs: AoPS Prealgebra, ch. 7 (Ratios, Conversions, and Rates)

cards.title: What does $p\%$ mean as a fraction and as a decimal?
cards.body:
$p\%$ means $p$ per hundred: $p\% = \frac{p}{100}$, and as a decimal you move the point two places left.

A **percent** is a ratio whose second part is 100.

Example: $37.5\% = \frac{37.5}{100} = 0.375 = \frac{3}{8}$. To go the other way, divide to get the decimal, then multiply by 100: $\frac{3}{8} = 0.375 = 37.5\%$.

Tip: "of" means multiply. So $35\%$ of $80$ is $0.35 \cdot 80 = 28$.
cards.searchQuery: percent meaning per hundred convert percent decimal fraction

cards.title: 18 is 30% of what number? Type the number.
cards.body:
$60$

Write 30% as the decimal 0.30. Then 18 is 0.30 times the unknown whole, so the whole is $18 \div 0.30 = 60$.

Check: $0.30 \cdot 60 = 18$.

Why: finding a percent of the whole multiplies by the percent. Going from the part back to the whole undoes that, so you divide.

Watch out: do not multiply 18 by 0.30. That finds 30% of 18, which is 5.4, not the whole.
cards.searchQuery: find the whole from a part and a percent

cards.title: What is the formula for **percent change** from an old value to a new value?
cards.body:
$\text{percent change} = \dfrac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}} \cdot 100\%$

A positive result is a **percent increase**; a negative result means a **percent decrease** of that size.

Example: a price going from 40 to 46 changes by $\frac{6}{40} = 0.15$, a 15% increase. A price going from 50 to 40 changes by $\frac{-10}{50} = -0.2$, a 20% decrease.

Watch out: always divide by the old value. Going from 40 up to 50 is a 25% increase, but going from 50 back down to 40 is only a 20% decrease.
cards.searchQuery: percent change formula new minus old over old

cards.title: A quantity rises by $p\%$ or falls by $p\%$. What **multiplier** gives the new value?
cards.body:
Rise: multiply by $1 + \frac{p}{100}$. Fall: multiply by $1 - \frac{p}{100}$.

A **multiplier** is the number you multiply the old amount by to get the new amount.

Why: the new amount is 100% of the old plus (or minus) $p\%$ of it, which is $\left(1 \pm \frac{p}{100}\right)$ times the old.

Example: a 15% rise uses the multiplier 1.15, and a 15% fall uses 0.85. An item priced at $60$ dollars goes to $60 \cdot 1.15 = 69$ dollars after a 15% rise, or $60 \cdot 0.85 = 51$ dollars after a 15% fall.
cards.searchQuery: percent increase decrease multiplier 1.15 0.85

cards.title: Why does a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease not bring you back to the start?
cards.body:
The second change is 20% of a different, larger amount, so the multipliers multiply: $1.2 \cdot 0.8 = 0.96$, a net 4% decrease.

Example: start at 100. A 20% rise gives 120. A 20% fall takes off $0.20 \cdot 120 = 24$, which is more than the 20 you added, leaving 96.

Key idea: successive percent changes multiply their multipliers. They do not add their percents.
cards.searchQuery: successive percent changes do not add multiply multipliers

cards.title: After a 15% raise, a salary is 46,000 dollars. What was the salary before the raise? Type the number of dollars.
cards.body:
$40000$

A 15% raise means new salary = old salary times 1.15. So the old salary is $46000 \div 1.15 = 40000$.

Check: $40000 \cdot 1.15 = 46000$.

Watch out: you can't just take 15% off the new salary. $46000 \cdot 0.85 = 39100$ is wrong, because the 15% was a percent of the old salary, not of the new one.
cards.searchQuery: find original amount after percent increase reverse multiplier

cards.title: A rate rises from 4% to 6%. Why is it wrong to call that a 2% increase?
cards.body:
It is a rise of 2 **percentage points**, but a 50% increase in the rate: $\frac{6 - 4}{4} = 0.5$.

A **percentage point** is the difference between two percents. Percent change compares the change to the starting value; a percentage-point change just subtracts.

Example: if 4% of people have a condition and later 6% do, the share went up 2 percentage points, and 1.5 times as many people have it.

Watch out: headlines often blur the two. Ask "percent of what?" to tell which is meant.
cards.searchQuery: percentage point vs percent change difference
